3. The plaintiffs challenged all the three dispositions on various grounds, but the one relevant for our consideration, in that Sujan Bibi was a pardanashin lady, and she was also old and illiterate, and so the disposition of property made by her in favour of her grandsons, defendants 1 and 2 in order to be valid, required to be proved by the grandsons that the lady made intelligent execution of the documents, and that in so doing she got independent and disinterested advice. The trial Court held, that the grandsons (defendants 1 and 2) carried burden of proving that the lady got independent advice before the transaction, and they failed to call any evidence to discharge this onus of proof. On fact, the trial Court held that the grandsons obtained the documents by exercise of undue influence. On appeal the Court of appeal below reversing this decision held that when the pardanashin lady though illiterate was capable of managing her own affairs, the onus was not on the defendants, the beneficiaries of deeds, to prove that the documents were read over to Sujan Bibi and she executed those document after understanding the contents thereof and nature of transaction under them, and the onus shifts on the plaintiffs to prove that the documents were not explained to Sujan Bibi, and that she executed them without understanding the nature of the transactions under the documents. He held that plaintiffs had failed to discharge their onus. 

 "According to the established principle, in case of a document executed by an illiterate pardanashin lady, the burden lies on those who seek to hold the lady to the terms of her deed to satisfy the Court on evidence that the deed was actually executed by her with full understanding of what she was about to do that she had full knowledge of the nature and effect of the transaction into which she is said to have entered; and that she had independent and disinterested advice in the matter." 

 7. The main considerations are two. First, whether proof of an independent advice is indispensable in case of transaction where the protection to a pardanashin woman is available; and, secondly, whether the rule of special onus laid down for the protection of pardanashin woman can be extended to a person other than the pardanashin lady but claiming interest through her. 

 10. The earliest case is that of Tacoor Deen Tewary vs. Nawab Syed Ali Hossain Khan 1 I.A. 192. it was held by the Privy Council that where a pardanashin lady, lying apart from her relations and natural advisers, makes a deed in favour of a person who has, on some occasions, acted as her man of business, the strongest proof ought to be given by him that the transaction was a real and bonafide one, and was fully understood by the lady whose property is dealt with. It was further observed that in a suit for setting aside deeds some evidence ought to be given by the plaintiff in order to impeach such deeds and is not entitled, merely on the proof of heir ship, to throw on the defendant the burden of showing a better title. It was a suit by a plaintiff in whose favour the lady executed a sale deed which he sought to enforce against the heirs of the lady. It is to be observed that the lady also challenged the document as fraudulent and fabricated and in that context the observation set out above was made by the Privy Council. 

 12. The next decision is in the case of Mirza Sajjad Husain vs Nawab Wazir Ali Khan 39 I.A. 156. Here the suit was brought by the plaintiffs praying for declaration that all the property comprised was a waqf and the plaintiffs were trustees under the deed and claimed for possession and there it appeared that the conveyance was made by a pardanashin woman under which the plaintiff's claimed to be trustees. It was held that the onus was, upon them to show that the transaction had been explained to the pardanashin lady and that she understood it. It was observed that the onus of proof has not been discharged by the plaintiff-appellants and the Privy Council in that view dismissed the appeal. An observation was made in this case following the authority of Tacoor Deen Tewary vs, Nawab Syed Ali Hossain Khan 1 I.A. 192 and Shambati Koeri vs. Argo Bibi 29 I.A 131, stating that it is well-known rule of the Privy Council that in case of the deeds and powers executed by pardanashin ladies, it is a prerequisite that those who rely upon them should satisfy the Court that they have been explained to and understood by those who executed them. 

 13. In the case of Kali Baksh Singh vs. Ram Gopal Singh 41 I A. 23, the question before the Privy Council was as to the validity of the deed of gift purported to have been executed on September 24, 1903 by Balraj Kuar, a literate pardanashin lady. The suit was for a decree for actual proprietary right and of possession of certain shares in villages Paraganah Salon, and the claim constituted in a demand for cancellation of the deed of gift aforesaid. The deed stood in favour or Ganga Baksh Singh„ son of Kali Baksha Singh. The plaintiffs were distant relation of the husband of the pardanashin lady. The gift was in favour of the son of the Mukter of the lady. In the context of these facts, it was held by the Privy Council, on a review of some earlier decisions, that there is no absolute rule of law that a deed of gift by a pardanashin woman is invalid in the absence of proof that she had independent advice. The absence of independent advice is a fact to be taken into consideration on the issue as to whether the grantor thoroughly understood the transaction and carried it out deliberately of her own free will. If a review of the facts including the nature of the transaction, the training and habit of mind of the grantor, and the proximate circumstances affecting the execution, leads to the conclusion that independent advice would not have made any difference in the result, then the gift should be declared valid. 

 22. Now remains to consider a recent decision on the subject given by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Kharbuja Kuer vs. Jang Bahadur A. I. R. 1963 S. C. 1203, The suit was brought by a pardanashin lady for nullification of a deed of agreement for maintenance and the dispute was between the parties to the agreement directly. In this case the authority of Faridun Nisa vs. Mukhtar Ahmed (30 C. W. N. 337-52 I. A. 342 was cited and the observation made therein regarding the protection given to the pardanashin lady was quoted. It was observed that the rule evolved for the protection of pardanashin ladies should not be confused with other doctrines such as fraud, duress and actual undue influence, which apply to all persons whether they are pardanashin ladies or not. In this case the authority of Hemchandra vs Suradhani Debya (A. I R. 194 0 P. C. 134) was also cited. It was then observed that shortly it may be stated thus: The burden of proof shall always rest upon the person who seeks to sustain a transaction entered into with a pardanashin lady to establish that the said document was executed by her after clearly understanding the nature of the transaction. It should be established that it was not only her physical act but also her mental act. The burden can be discharged not only by proving that the document was explained to her and that she understood it, but also by other evidence, direct and circumstantial." 

 24. If in a case of a transfer by a pardanashin lady a dispute arises as to its validity, the onus is always on the party who seeks to hold the transferor to the terms of the deed to satisfy the Court on evidence that she substantially understood the disposition and she executed the deed with full understanding of what she was doing and of the nature and effect of the transaction, It is to be observed that independent advice by itself is not an essential burden to be discharged, unless there are some special circumstances calling for its application, in that the donee or the transferee stood in a position of active confidence or had fiduciary relationship with the pardanashin lady. It is only in such eases, the donee or transferee will carry the additional burden or to prove that the lady had independent and disinterested advice from persons other than the recipient of the document. 

 26. We are, therefore, of the view that this special rule of onus of proof will apply in a suit where the validity of the document executed by a pardanashin lady is in question and she herself, is a party to the suit, either as plaintiff or defendant. This rule cannot be extended to any other person other than the transferor or executant, viz, the pardanashin lady herself. 

 27. We now revert to the two questions to test their soundness. As to the first question namely, whether the learned Single Judge in the Ayani Dasi was correct in observing that whenever a transaction between a pardanashin lady is in question, the recipient of the deed carries in addition the burden of proving that she had independent and disinterested advice cannot be sustained and to that extent the decision is not correct exposition of law. 

 29. To turn to the finding of the learned Judge of the High Court on this question, we find that he has approved the finding of the first appellate Court that in the present case independent advice was not at all necessary in the facts and circumstances of the case, because, the donor was making a gift in favour of her deceased daughter's sons and also found that the defendants 1 and 2 the recipients under the three documents were the grandsons of Sujan Bibi. He also found that she was not that illiterate as was tried to be shown. It was found that Sujan Bibi used to manage her properties in her possession either through her servant or her neighbour. We, however, refrain from observing on the other questions involved in the suit as no leave has been granted on them. It is therefore, clear that the finding of the Court of appeal below affirmed by the learned Single Judge is that the pardanashin lady in the case did execute the documents by putting her thumb impression consciously after fully understanding the purport of the disposition. On this finding, the dispute regarding the special onus of proof lying on the defendants vanishes. However, it is to be observed the plaintiff-1 not being the pardanashin lady the special rule of onus does not apply. As to the general onus, the finding is conclusive on a discussion of evidence that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that Sujan Bibi executed the documents either under undue influence of defendants 1 and 2, or she executed them without understanding the nature of the transaction. On the finding, the plaintiffs cannot succeed.
